verdict.rationale: ScrapingBee lets developers control when HTML is returned. Its headless browser can wait for a CSS/XPath selector before returning, and JS scenarios can insert explicit waits (e.g. 'wait': 1000) before content comes back. Default resource blocking and optional ad blocking trade completeness for speed. Missing for 10: no documented standalone wait-in-milliseconds or request-timeout parameter, no network-idle style return condition, no documented latency figures showing the tradeoff, and no independent or hands-on corroboration.

support.subject: As a developer, I can trade off latency against completeness by controlling exactly when content is returned

citations.quote: Our headless browsers will wait for the CSS / Xpath selector passed in the parameter before returning the HTML.
If you want to interact with pages you want to scrape before we return your the HTML you can add JavaScript scenario to your API call.
By default, and to speed up requests, ScrapingBee blocks all images and CSS in the scraped page, but to scrape them, use `block_resources=false`
To avoid scraping them (e.g.,to speed up your request), use `block_ads=true`
